- **The gated live-PostgreSQL test suite runs green for the first time â€” one real grant gap and five latent test defects** ([#1551]) â€” the nightly `darling-pg` job had never actually executed: it was added July 2, but scheduled nightly runs execute the workflow file from `main`, which predates the job entirely, so its first real run was a manual dispatch on July 17 â€” which failed wall-to-wall. Fixed, in dependency order: **(1) the throwaway cluster now initdbs its superuser as `darling`** (it used `postgres`, but the V8 schema-split migration runs `CREATE SCHEMA ... AUTHORIZATION darling`, so every fresh-store migration died with `role "darling" does not exist`); with migrations unblocked, the suite exposed **(2) a real viewer-role grant gap** â€” V18 added `alert_delivery_mode_override` to `config_monitored_servers` without adding it to `DarlingManagedRoles`' fail-closed non-secret column list, so a read-only `viewer` seat (including a remote network viewer, whose pg_hba default is `viewer`) was silently denied the per-server delivery-mode override column; the live ratchet test caught it exactly as designed, and the column is now granted. The remaining four were test defects that had never run: **(3)** the two `SeedAndRead ... AgainstScratchPostgres` round-trips assumed an isolated store but ran against the shared CI database, where `SeedIfEmptyAsync` correctly no-ops after any earlier test seeds â€” each now mints (and drops) its own scratch database; **(4)** the system_health planted-events test INSERTed a `collection_id` column that never existed on `system_health_events` (its id column is `system_health_event_id`); **(5)** the managed-bootstrap E2E derived its expected `max_worker_processes` from the catalog count while the product correctly sizes from `TimescaleSupport.HypertableCount` (catalog **plus** `collection_log`); and **(6)** the TimescaleDB E2E asserted `collection_log` becomes a hypertable via the V23 migration alone, but V23 is deliberately a guarded upgrade fast-path that skips when the extension does not exist yet â€” the test now exercises `EnsureCollectionLogHypertableAsync`, the authoritative runtime path the service calls on every start (which is also how a fresh managed store converges). No collector, store, or viewer behavior changes; the only product change is the viewer-role column grant.


- **Darling viewer: query-tab plan menus fixed â€” no greyed-out verbs, right-click acts on the clicked row, and the Regressions / live Active Queries grids get plan access** ([#1543]) â€” several issues surfaced during live testing: (1) the shared plan context menu showed **greyed-out** "View Cached Plan" / "Get Actual Plan (re-run)" on grids whose rows can't satisfy them (Top Procedures, Query Store), so those verbs now **hide** rather than disable (per-row visibility binding) and each grid shows only the verbs that work; (2) the viewer never enabled **right-click-selects-row** (Lite and the Dashboard do), so a right-click could act on a *different* row than the one highlighted â€” its plan handlers read `CurrentItem` â€” now wired app-wide in `App.OnStartup`; (3) the **Query Store Regressions** grid had no plan options at all (its rows aggregate across plans, so there is no single stored plan to view) â€” it now offers **"Get Actual Plan (re-run)"** by QueryId via the same service path the Query Store history window uses, and the Query Store grid gains it too; (4) the live **Current Active Queries** grid lacked the right-click plan menu its stored sibling has â€” it now uses the snapshot row style, so Estimated / Live plan access is available by right-click. Stale docs corrected (the Regressions "no plan surface" note and the history windows' "Get Actual Plan is dropped"). Darling only; capability-pin grid-style + menu-command baselines updated.
- **Darling viewer: the first click on an unsorted grid column now sorts descending, and header-copy plus middle-click panning work on every grid** ([#1541]) â€” the viewer's data grids use an explicit `DarkGrid` style that carried no `BasedOn`, so it fully *replaced* the implicit `TargetType="DataGrid"` style instead of extending it, silently dropping the three attached behaviors that style contributes: `DataGridSortBehavior.SortDescendingFirst` (performance triage wants the largest CPU / duration / reads on top, so the first header click should sort descending rather than WPF's default ascending), `DataGridClipboardBehavior.FixHeaderCopy`, and `ScrollPanBehavior.EnableMiddleClickPanning`. Every query-tab grid (Top Queries, Top Procedures, Query Store, Regressions, snapshots) plus the FinOps and main-window grids therefore sorted ascending-first on the first click and lacked the copy / pan behaviors; Lite was unaffected because its grids use the implicit style. The three behaviors are now re-declared on all four `DarkGrid` definitions â€” a targeted setter add rather than `BasedOn`, which would also inherit the implicit style's vertical gridlines / clipping / padding and change the grids' appearance. Darling only.
- **Charts: finish the window-pin campaign so trend charts stay pinned to the selected window** ([#1540]) â€” Collection Health > Duration Trends still AutoScaled on load in both apps (the one chart #1483/#1484/#1487 missed), and every chart's Revert menu item + double-click AutoScaled to the data range (re-introducing the ~10% side dead-space on any interaction) instead of restoring the window pin. Both now pin X to the settable window (+ auto-Y); the Query Heatmap's categorical axis is unaffected.
- **Lite and Darling: Azure SQL DB deadlock and blocked-process capture now covers EVERY monitored database, not just the connection's own** ([#1346], [#1535]) â€” reported by a user whose nightly regression tests deadlock across ~50 Azure SQL databases while the Deadlocks page stayed empty even after the [#1251] fix unblocked the ring-buffer read. On Azure SQL DB these captures are *database-scoped* Extended Events sessions, and both the session-create and the ring-buffer read ran only on the connection's `Initial Catalog` â€” so a deadlock in any *other* database of the logical server was invisible by construction, while Azure's own server-wide `dl` telemetry (the user's proof query) showed them plainly. Meanwhile query stats, file I/O, index/object stats and database sizes already looped every database, so the app's own behavior taught users to expect whole-server coverage. **Both XE collectors now declare `RunsPerDatabase` on Azure**: the session is ensured and its ring buffer read once per monitored database (master skipped â€” logical master can't host database-scoped sessions; `ExcludedDatabases` honored via the shared list), exactly like the other per-database collectors. **Each database gets its own watermark** (new `PerDatabaseWatermarkColumn` contract on the shared definitions, honored by both hosts' runners): the sessions dispatch independently, so under the old single server-wide watermark one busy database's newer event would silence another database's older event still sitting in its ring buffer. `deadlocks` gains a trailing `database_name` column as that key (DuckDB v46 / Postgres V27 append + pinned-view refresh; `blocked_process_reports` has carried it since introduction) â€” on the per-database path both collectors stamp it with the capture database itself (a database-scoped session only captures its own database, and a row whose event XML carries no `currentdbname` could otherwise never advance its database's watermark, re-inserting every cycle until it aged out of the ring buffer); server-scoped platforms keep the victim/blocked process's `currentdbname` from the existing graph parse. **The [#1251] benign path also grew a read-back check**: a benign "already exists" (25631) proves the session exists, but NOT that this principal can see it â€” the reader joins `sys.dm_xe_database_sessions`, and a session invisible there (created by another principal, or present-but-stopped) reads zero rows forever while the collector records SUCCESS, the exact silent-empty shape of the report. After a benign error the session is now probed in the reader's own DMV and an invisible one is dropped and recreated under this principal; failure isolation is per database (one broken database never blocks the rest), and only all-databases-failed surfaces the collector unhealthy ([#1086] semantics). Darling's on-prem ensure additionally stops letting a benign deadlock-session collision skip the blocked-process ensure (each capture now ensures under its own benign filter), and the per-database "session verified" log lines drop to Debug so 50 databases don't write 100 Info lines per cycle. Grids need no changes â€” the per-process deadlock rows already display each process's database via the shared graph parser. Lite + Darling
- **Lite and Darling: an Azure SQL DB outage no longer permanently wedges database-scoped collection until the app is restarted** ([#1506]) â€” reported by a user monitoring Azure SQL DB from a machine whose public IP rotates daily: each time it changed, the server's firewall rule stopped matching and connections were rejected; re-adding the rule brought the server back, but Lite kept collecting nothing until it was restarted. **The cause was an error-classification bug, not a connection bug.** `IsMasterAccessDeniedError` decided whether a login is permanently unable to read `master` â€” the [#857] case, where a contained user exists only in a user database and database-scoped collectors must fall back to the connection's own catalog â€” but its error list also contained two errors that describe *reachability*, not *rights*: **40615** ("client with IP address â€¦ is not allowed to access the server", i.e. the firewall rejection this user hit every day) and **40613** ("not currently available, please retry later"). Worse, the resulting verdict was cached in a per-server dictionary that was only ever written `true`, so a single unlucky moment during an outage permanently demoted a perfectly healthy server. The codebase openly contradicted itself: 40613 sat in `RetryHelper.TransientErrorNumbers` as *retryable* while simultaneously being treated as *permanently fatal*. **Three fixes, applied to both SKUs.** (1) Both reachability errors are **removed** from the master-access list â€” a firewall rejection is not evidence about `master`, and falling back to a user database is futile anyway since the same rule blocks that connection too; they now propagate as ordinary collector errors: logged, visible in `collection_log`, retried next cycle. 4060 and 18456 stay, because a contained user genuinely does get them when opening `master`. (2) The verdict becomes a **throttle, not a life sentence** â€” it records *when* it was formed, expires after 15 minutes, and is **discarded outright the moment a server returns from an outage** (Lite tracks the offlineâ†’online edge in its scheduler loop; Darling hangs it off the existing `TryConnectAsync` connection edge that already fires "Server Restored"), because a judgement formed while a server was failing is untrustworthy by construction. A login that truly cannot see `master` still only re-probes 4x/hour, and the throttle is skipped entirely when there is no fallback database to throttle *to* â€” honouring it there would guarantee 15 minutes of failure without ever attempting to recover. (3) The failure is no longer **silent**: when master can't be enumerated *and* the connection has no target database to fall back on (`InitialCatalog` defaults to `master`, and a single-DB list of `master` is empty), every database-scoped collector iterated an empty list, wrote zero rows, and recorded **SUCCESS** â€” so the status bar cheerfully read "Collection: Running / Collectors: N OK" while nothing whatsoever was being collected. That case now throws, landing a real error in `collection_log` that names the fix (set a Database for the server); a test pins that the message can't be mistaken for the MFA-cancellation filter that would downgrade it back to a silent SKIPPED. **The root enabler was duplication:** Lite and Darling each carried their own copy of these error lists, which is precisely how the bug was ported from one to the other, and the transient list lived in Lite where no Darling test could see it. Both lists now live in one shared, dependency-free `SqlErrorClassification` (plain `int`s, no SqlClient), so they cannot be edited in one SKU and not the other â€” and the **disjointness invariant is asserted from both test suites**: no error number may be simultaneously "retry this" and "give up forever", which is the bug class itself and would have caught this at authoring time. Master enumeration also gains a retry it never had (a blip now costs a slower cycle instead of an ERROR row â€” though note it cannot itself prevent a verdict, since retryable and verdict-forming errors are disjoint by construction). Lite + Darling
- **Dashboard and Lite: the server-list version display no longer risks a crash on a two-part version string** ([#1510]) â€” six spots across the two apps' server-list / landing / health views hand-rolled `Version.TryParse(v, out p) ? new Version(p.Major, p.Minor, p.Build).ToString() : v`, which carries a latent throw: `Version.TryParse("3.1")` succeeds with `Build == -1`, and `new Version(3, 1, -1)` throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`. They are consolidated into one shared `PerformanceMonitor.Ui.VersionText` (`Parse` clamps `Build` up from -1 and strips SemVer `+build`/`-prerelease` suffixes; `Normalize` gives the three-part display form) â€” the UI-layer twin of the installer's `ScriptProvider.TryParseVersionCore` hardening from [#1498], now pinned by regression tests in the CI-wired `Lite.Tests`. Behavior-preserving for every realistic input (a real version or a status string); only the two-part throw changes.
- **Clean install is Azure SQL Managed Instance-safe, and a failed drop no longer leaves the database bricked** ([#1498]) â€” the clean-install teardown ran `ALTER DATABASE ... SET SINGLE_USER WITH ROLLBACK IMMEDIATE` before `DROP DATABASE` to evict other connections. `SINGLE_USER` is non-modifiable on Azure SQL Managed Instance (`SERVERPROPERTY('EngineEdition') = 8`), so the whole teardown batch died on that line there; it is now gated to box SQL Server (MI drops directly, relying on there being no other sessions, which an installer teardown normally guarantees). And because `SINGLE_USER` and `DROP` are two separate autocommitted statements, a `DROP` that failed (another session racing the single-user slot) or hit the client command-timeout/cancel *after* `SINGLE_USER` committed left the database online but stranded in `SINGLE_USER` â€” semi-bricked. The teardown now restores `MULTI_USER` best-effort on a fresh connection before re-raising the original error (a client-attention timeout is invisible to a server-side `TRY/CATCH`, so this has to be C#-side); the Dashboard's server-drop path warns if that restore itself fails. Applies to `InstallationService.CleanInstallAsync` and the Dashboard's "remove server" drop; the SQL constructs were verified against Microsoft Learn for both box SQL Server and Managed Instance.
- **CLI installer: a password beginning with `--` gets a clear message instead of a misleading "password required"** ([#1498]) â€” a value like `--h7x` passed as the SQL-auth password is indistinguishable from a flag, so the positional-argument filter dropped it and the run then reported *"Password is required"* â€” for a password that *was* supplied. The error now adds a targeted note (only when a `--`-token that is not a recognized flag actually appeared) explaining that such a password must go through `PM_SQL_PASSWORD`. The parsing is unchanged â€” deliberately, since accepting `--`-prefixed values positionally is what would make a mistyped flag become a password.
- **Dashboard: a failed upgrade migration no longer stamps the database as successfully upgraded** ([#1498]) â€” `AddServerDialog` logged *"Upgrade failures detected. Continuing with full installation to ensure consistency..."* when an `upgrades/*` script failed, ran the full install over the partially-upgraded database anyway, and then wrote an `installation_history` row using `InstallationResult.Success` â€” which is `FilesFailed == 0` for the **install files only** and excludes upgrade failures entirely. That row was permanent damage: version detection reads the most recent `installation_status = 'SUCCESS'` row, and upgrade discovery only offers hops newer than the detected version, so the failed migration was stamped SUCCESS at the target version, the server then reported as current with the `ALTER`s never applied, and the hop was **never offered again** â€” silent schema drift recoverable only by a clean install. `ExecuteAllUpgradesAsync` already documented the contract ("*the caller aborts the whole install when totalFailureCount > 0*") and the CLI installer honored it; only the Dashboard's single-server path did not. The dialog now aborts on upgrade failure without running the install or writing a history row â€” leaving no `SUCCESS` row is exactly what makes the hop get re-offered, and upgrade scripts are written with guarded `ALTER`s so a re-run after fixing the error resumes cleanly â€” and folds the upgrade counts into the history write, matching the CLI. Relatedly, `ScriptProvider.FilterUpgrades` now throws on a version that is present but has no parseable numeric core instead of silently returning "no upgrades needed" (an empty result must never be the answer to "I could not read the version you gave me" â€” that path is what let a status string like `"Unreachable"` skip every migration while reporting zero failures), and `ExecuteAllUpgradesAsync` reports that as a failure so callers abort through the existing contract rather than hitting an unhandled exception. The **CLI**'s abort was itself nested inside `if (upgradeCount > 0)`, so a discovery failure (which reports zero hops) slipped past it â€” the CLI printed *"No pending upgrades found."* and ran the whole install; the abort now sits outside that block. Two latent version-parsing bugs the strict parse would have detonated are closed at the same choke point: `Version.TryParse("3.1")` succeeds with `Build == -1`, which the `Version` ctor rejects (now clamped), and `GetAppVersion` strips a `+metadata` suffix but not `-prerelease` â€” so a `3.2.0-rc1` `<InformationalVersion>` would have hard-aborted every upgrade. `FilterUpgrades` now normalizes SemVer suffixes at the choke point rather than relying on the seven call sites that each hand-strip them, mirroring `SingleInstanceDecision.ParseProductVersion`. The two decisions that can corrupt the ledger â€” "is installing safe?" (`InstallGuard`) and "are a repair's file failures the expected kind?" (`RepairOutcome`) â€” are extracted into `Installer.Core` and shared by both surfaces rather than hand-copied, and pinned by regression cases in `Installer.Tests`, which is CI-wired (`Dashboard.Tests` is not, so tests placed there could never fail a PR). One caveat worth recording: the ledger-lost probe is SQL, so its only test lives in `VersionDetectionTests`, which CI excludes because it needs a real SQL Server â€” that query was verified by hand against SQL Server 2022, but it cannot fail a PR. Found while reviewing [#963].
- **Dashboard: a failed version check no longer reinstalls over an existing database and reports it as up to date** ([#1498]) â€” `AddServerDialog`'s pre-install discovery called `GetInstalledVersionAsync` with the *soft*, null-returning overload. That method's own comment names the hazard: the installer passes `throwOnError: true` so "a transient/permission error can't be mistaken for 'database absent' and silently trigger a fresh install over an existing database (no upgrades, then logged as SUCCESS â€” the #538 hazard)", and only *soft callers* (the version column) keep the null fallback. But this call is not the version column â€” it is the discovery that decides install-vs-upgrade, the same class of caller as the CLI. So a connection timeout, a database left `OFFLINE`/`RESTORING`, or a permissions blip came back as `null`, read as "no database", and dropped the dialog into the fresh-install path: every migration skipped, install scripts run over the existing database, and `installation_history` stamped `SUCCESS` at the target version â€” stranding every pending hop exactly as above. Discovery now fails loudly and the dialog enters a new "status unknown" state that hides the install button and explains why; an `_installBlockedReason` guard also hard-blocks the install path, so the protection is structural rather than depending on a hidden button. The version is re-read â€” and the safety verdict re-run â€” against the connection the installer is about to *write* to, since the server box stays editable after a connection test.
- **A non-destructive repair path, so aborting on a failed migration doesn't leave you stuck** ([#1498]) â€” an upgrade script can fail *because* an object it `ALTER`s is missing or damaged, and before the abort above, the full install running afterwards would quietly recreate it. With the abort in place the only remaining escape hatch was Clean Install, which drops the database. **Dashboard** gains a "Repair: reinstall objects, skip upgrade scripts" option in Advanced Options (mutually exclusive with clean install; the upgrade-abort message now points at it), and the **CLI installer** gains `--repair` (mutually exclusive with `--reinstall`). Both run the idempotent install scripts *without* running migrations, so missing objects come back and the pending upgrade can then be re-run. Critically, a repair *that skips pending migrations* writes **no** `installation_history` row: it changes no version, and that table is the version ledger â€” echoing back a version we merely *read* is how a guess becomes a fact (`GetInstalledVersionAsync` returns the `0.0.0` sentinel as a fallback meaning "unknown, try every upgrade", and persisting that as a `SUCCESS` row would make the guess true). Writing nothing leaves the previous row as the version of record, so the pending upgrade is still offered. Note that a repair against a database with pending migrations is *expected* to report errors on a few procedures: the install scripts compile against the current schema (`install/23_process_blocked_process_xml.sql` reads a column the `3.0.0-to-3.1.0` migration adds) and `ALTER PROCEDURE` binds columns at compile time, so those objects cannot compile until the upgrade runs. A failed `CREATE OR ALTER` leaves the old body intact, nothing is damaged, and the upgrade recompiles them â€” so the "run the upgrade next" handoff is deliberately not gated on a clean repair.
- **`--repair` exit-code contract** ([#1498]) â€” a repair with a *pending upgrade* exits **0** even with failed files, because those failures are the expected compile errors described above; reporting them as a failure sent operators reaching for `--reinstall`, which drops the database. A repair with **no** pending upgrade has no such excuse, so a failure there still exits non-zero. A third case: when the server's recorded version cannot be read at all, the failures cannot be excused (exit non-zero) but an upgrade *is* still offered â€” those are two different questions, and answering both with one flag told operators "already at the current version, so there is no upgrade to apply" for a server with every hop pending. `--repair` also now refuses when there is no installation to repair, rather than silently performing a full fresh install and stamping the target version on a mistyped server.
- **Dashboard: retyping the server name no longer leaves the previous server's answers on screen** ([#1498]) â€” the Add/Edit Server box stays editable while the connection status, installed version, safety verdict and the Advanced Options checkboxes all describe whichever server was last *checked*. Nothing re-read the box, so every one of those could end up describing a different server than the one named on screen, and one of them is destructive: a ticked "clean install" (which runs `DROP DATABASE PerformanceMonitor` and drops the Agent jobs and Extended Events sessions) survived a retarget and could fire against a server that was never consented to, with no confirmation. Each verdict is now stamped with the server it was actually read from, and the dialog refuses to render one whose stamp no longer matches the box â€” a single structural check, rather than a re-check remembered at each of the dozen places that display or act on it. Related, from the same root: a connection test still in flight when an install started could wake up afterwards and republish its *pre-install* verdict over the finished result (restoring "Upgrade Now" on a server that had just been upgraded); **Save** could close the dialog the instant an install landed, which under SQL authentication skipped the monitoring-credentials prompt entirely and persisted the *installer's* account â€” routinely `sa` â€” as the ongoing monitoring login; and **Save** would skip the connection test altogether after an install, so a name typed into the box afterwards was saved without ever being contacted.
- **Cancelling an install is reported as a cancellation, not a failure â€” at every stage** ([#1498]) â€” a cancelled `SqlCommand` faults with `SqlException`, not `OperationCanceledException`, so two windows in the installer were counting a cancel as an ordinary failure and returning a normal result instead of surfacing the cancel: the clean-install teardown (before any install file runs), and the install file loop itself (a cancel during a *critical* file, which aborts the loop, or during the *last* file, which ends it â€” neither returns to the loop-top cancellation check). Both now convert a cancel into `OperationCanceledException` so the caller takes its cancellation path rather than announcing *"Installation completed with N error(s)."*
- **Cancelling a clean install no longer reports success over a database it just dropped** ([#1498]) â€” a clean install drops the three SQL Agent jobs, both Extended Events sessions, and then the database itself (`SET SINGLE_USER WITH ROLLBACK IMMEDIATE`, `DROP DATABASE`) *before* the first install script runs. That was the single most destructive window in the installer, and it was the only one with no cancellation check in front of it â€” the first `ThrowIfCancellationRequested` sat *after* it. Worse, a cancelled `SqlCommand` faults with `SqlException`, not `OperationCanceledException`, so the clean-install error handler swallowed the cancel as an ordinary failure and returned **normally**: the caller's cancellation path never ran. Clicking **Cancel Install** mid-drop produced *"Installation completed with 1 error(s)"* over a database that was already gone, restored the version verdict the dialog had deliberately discarded for safety, and â€” because **Save** skips the connection test once that verdict is stamped â€” let the server be saved without ever being reconnected to. A cancel is now surfaced as a cancel, and a clean install that *fails* is treated the same way: no history row, no verdict, the install log left on screen, and installing blocked until the server is re-checked. Pinned by regression tests, which is possible because the fix lives in `Installer.Core` rather than in the dialog.
- **Dashboard: "Save" is no longer enabled on a server with no PerformanceMonitor database** ([#1498]) â€” the `Connected_NoDatabase` state disables Save deliberately: the intended paths are **Install Now**, or the explicit *"Skip, just add server"* link (which re-enables Save itself). A button-gating change made while fixing an unrelated overlapping-probe bug re-enabled Save unconditionally after every status check, which handed that consent away on the most ordinary path in the product â€” point at a bare instance, click Check for Updates, read *"No PerformanceMonitor database found"*, and Save is live. It is also the default button, so **Enter** would commit a server the Dashboard can read nothing from.
- **Dashboard: cancelling an edit no longer silently renames the server you were editing** ([#1498]) â€” the Add/Edit Server dialog writes its fields straight into the `ServerConnection` object it was handed, and in edit mode that object *is* the one `ServerManager` holds â€” not a copy. Clicking **Save** and then closing the dialog (ESC, Cancel, the X) while the connection test was still running let the test finish and complete the save anyway: the dialog was gone, `ShowDialog` had already returned "cancelled", and the caller never persisted anything â€” but the live object had already been mutated in place, and it reached disk on its own the next time any server's `last_connected` was written. A `PROD01` retargeted to `TEST99` and abandoned would come back as `TEST99` under `PROD01`'s id and credentials, and `PROD01` would stop being monitored, with nothing on screen ever having said so.
- **Dashboard: a failed or cancelled clean install no longer hides the install log** ([#1498]) â€” the clean-install path deliberately discards the pre-install version (the database is about to be dropped, so a verdict describing it would be a lie), and the "no verdict to restore" branch that handles that returned *before* the line that re-shows the installation panel â€” which the surrounding code had collapsed. The install log is the only place the actual SQL error text appears, and `DROP DATABASE` runs *before* the install scripts, so a cancel or failure at any point afterwards left the user with a dropped database, a single exception message, and no log. That branch also told them "this server's installed version was not read", which on that path is false â€” it was read, and deliberately discarded.
- **Both installers now refuse to run over a database that is NEWER than the binary** ([#1498]) â€” an older Dashboard or CLI installing over a server someone upgraded with a newer build would run its own older scripts, reverting every `CREATE OR ALTER` procedure and view to the older definitions, and then record the **lower** version as `SUCCESS`. Because upgrade discovery only offers hops *newer* than the current version, that case yields zero hops and zero failures, so no abort caught it. Both surfaces now hard-block such a server, as they do a version that will not parse at all. In the Dashboard everything is blocked, clean install included, so the block message carries the whole escape route: update the Dashboard, or use the CLI installer's destructive `--reinstall` (which drops the database first, so there is nothing left to downgrade).
- **Lite and Darling: the collector gate surface is collapsed to ONE shared layer, so Darling stops attempting collectors it can't run (no-msdb / Azure SQL DB / pre-2016) every cycle** ([#1500]) â€” the direct sequel to the [#1492] RDS fix, closing the whole gating-drift class it exposed. Lite gated collectors in TWO places â€” the shared `ICollectorSchemaInfo.AppliesTo` (which Darling also honors) AND its own host-side `IsCollectorSupported` â€” while Darling gated ONLY on `AppliesTo`, so every gate Lite kept solely in the second layer was silently ignored by Darling: on a monitored login without msdb access Darling attempted `running_jobs`/`job_history`/`agent_status` every cycle (each failing 229/916 and polluting collection-health), on Azure SQL DB it attempted `server_config`/`trace_flags`, and neither SKU version-gated `query_stats`/`query_store` off a pre-2016 box in the shared layer. **The second layer is gone.** `CollectorTargetInfo` gains a `HasMsdbAccess` flag (default true = assume access, matching the probe's NULL semantics), populated in BOTH hosts from the `HAS_DBACCESS(N'msdb')` value each already probed â€” Darling had it on `ServerRuntime` but never wired it into the gate (the exact missing link), Lite reads it from `ServerConnectionStatus`. Each gate moved into the correct collector's shared `AppliesTo`, matching Lite's exact prior condition: `ServerConfigCollector`/`TraceFlagsCollector` â†’ `!IsAzureSqlDb`; `QueryStatsCollector`/`QueryStoreCollector` â†’ `SqlMajorVersion == 0 || >= 13 || IsAzureSqlDb || IsAzureManagedInstance`; `RunningJobsCollector`/`AgentStatusCollector` add `&& HasMsdbAccess` atop their existing `!IsAzureSqlDb && !IsAwsRds`, and `JobHistoryCollector` adds `&& HasMsdbAccess` atop `!IsAzureSqlDb` (still NOT RDS-gated â€” it never touches `syssessions`). `AppliesTo` is hoisted from `ICollectorDefinition<TRow>` up to the non-generic `ICollectorSchemaInfo` so `CollectorCatalog.AppliesTo(name, target)` can evaluate the gate by name without the row type â€” the ONE surface both SKUs consult. Lite's `IsCollectorSupported` is DELETED; `RunCollectorAsync` now calls `CollectorCatalog.AppliesTo` pre-dispatch, preserving its clean SKIPPED log (a genuine skip with no `collection_log` row, vs. the SUCCESS/0-rows a gated collector would otherwise record) â€” behavior-identical for Lite (same gates, relocated), and INTENTIONALLY corrective for Darling (it now skips these targets). The gate CONDITION lives ONLY in each definition's `AppliesTo`, so the two hosts can't drift on it again. Covered by extended per-collector `AppliesTo` tests (the msdb / config / version dimensions) plus a new `CollectorGateSurfacePinTests` that pins every moved gate's truth table (Azure SQL DB / AWS RDS / no-msdb / pre-2016) AND asserts `CollectorCatalog.AppliesTo(name, target)` agrees with each definition's own `AppliesTo` for every catalog collector across every target â€” the proof both SKUs now gate identically off one surface. Lite + Darling
- **Darling viewer: the collector-schedule presets now include `job_history`, `agent_status`, and `default_trace_events`, matching Lite** ([#1495]) â€” the viewer's Aggressive / Balanced / Low-Impact preset tables (`CollectorSchedulePresets.Presets`, duplicated byte-for-byte from Lite's `ScheduleManager.s_presets`) were missing these three collectors in **all three** presets, so applying a preset in the Darling schedule editor left them pinned at their code-default cadence instead of the preset's â€” a drift flagged during the [#1494] review. Each preset now carries the three at Lite's exact interval (Aggressive 2 min, Balanced 5 min, Low-Impact 15 min); retention is untouched (it lives in the shared `CollectorScheduleDefaults`, which already carried all three, so `BuildDefaultSchedule` was already correct â€” only the preset-apply path drifted). The class docstring promised "a Darling.Tests pin asserts they cannot drift from Lite's intervals," but no membership pin actually existed â€” the existing `Presets_OnlyReferenceKnownCollectors` only checks the reverse direction (no *unknown* collectors), which is why the missing three went uncaught. A new `Presets_CoverTheSamePinnedCollectorSet` test mirrors Lite's own `SchedulePresets_CoverTheSamePinnedCollectorSet`, pinning the full 27-collector membership of every preset so a future collector added to one SKU but not mirrored into all three Darling presets fails here instead of shipping silently. Darling
- **Lite: the `v_job_history` and `v_default_trace_events` archive views no longer double-count rows after a 512 MB emergency reset** ([#1492]) â€” both views `UNION` the hot table with the parquet archive, but `ArchiveService.ArchiveAllAndResetAsync` archives all hot data to parquet AND wipes `collection_log`, so the next cycle re-collects recent history into the hot store while parquet still holds it. The local surrogate prefix id is a per-process counter (`CollectionIdGenerator`), so the re-collected rows get brand-new ids and the plain `UNION ALL` showed each logical event twice. `CreateArchiveViewsAsync` now dedups each on its SQL-Server-side natural key via `QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY <key> ORDER BY collection_time DESC) = 1`, keeping the newest-collected (hot) copy â€” `job_history` on `(server_id, instance_id)` (the `sysjobhistory` identity that survives `sp_purge_jobhistory`), `default_trace_events` on `(server_id, event_time, event_sequence)` (the trace `EventSequence`, paired with `event_time` so it stays distinct across the server restarts that reset it). Other archivable tables are unaffected â€” normal archival keeps hot and parquet disjoint, so only these two re-collect over still-archived rows. Covered by a new `ArchiveViewDedupTests` that stages the archiveâ†’resetâ†’re-collect sequence and asserts each natural key appears exactly once with the hot copy winning. Lite
- **Lite and Darling: `agent_status` and `running_jobs` are now gated off AWS RDS in BOTH apps** ([#1492]) â€” Lite skipped these on RDS host-side (`IsCollectorSupported`), but the shared collector `AppliesTo` only knew about Azure SQL DB, so Darling â€” which gates purely on `AppliesTo` â€” ran them on RDS and logged a collection error every cycle. `sys.dm_server_services` (agent_status) reads OS/service-control state a managed RDS instance does not expose, and `running_jobs` joins `msdb.dbo.syssessions`, which RDS blocks with "SELECT permission was denied" even for the master login (the table requires sysadmin, which RDS never grants). `CollectorTargetInfo` gains an `IsAwsRds` flag (populated in both hosts from the existing `DB_ID('rdsadmin')` probe), and `AgentStatusCollector`/`RunningJobsCollector` `AppliesTo` now check `!IsAwsRds` so both hosts skip identically â€” mirroring how the Azure gate already lives in both `AppliesTo` and Lite's `IsCollectorSupported`. Also corrects a stale `RunningJobsCollector` doc comment that claimed RDS collects, and updates the two `AppliesTo` tests. `job_history` still collects on RDS (it reads only `sysjobhistory`/`sysjobs`/`syscategories`, which RDS exposes). Lite + Darling
- **Dashboard: the cross-app `ThemeParityTests` pass again â€” the Dashboard theme palettes are re-synced to Lite** ([#1492]) â€” a Lite-side CoolBreeze palette change ([#1441]) plus accumulated `Slicer*`/foreground drift left shared color keys differing across all three themes (CoolBreeze/Dark/Light), failing the parity guard. Every differing shared key in `Dashboard/Themes/{CoolBreeze,Dark,Light}Theme.xaml` â€” the `ForegroundMuted`/`ForegroundDim` colors and the `Slicer*`/`PlanPanelMuted` brushes â€” is realigned to Lite's value (Lite is the source of truth), mostly by mirroring Lite's `{StaticResource ...}` references so the palettes stay coupled rather than re-drifting on the next base-color tweak; this also fixes a couple of Dashboard-internal literals that didn't match the theme's own accent. Dashboard-only (a deprecated app, but a legitimate parity bug). Dashboard
- **Lite, Dashboard, and Darling: anomaly-engine remainder Stage A â€” baseline-quality gate, one-fact wait-profile detection, and honest no-baseline rendering** ([#1491]) â€” builds ON the SAFE #1486 floors/sigma-cap. Three coordinated changes across the triplicated anomaly engine (`Lite/Analysis/AnomalyDetector.cs` + `BaselineProvider.cs`, `Darling/PerformanceMonitor.Darling.Analysis/PgAnomalyDetector.cs` + `PgBaselineProvider.cs`, `Dashboard/Analysis/SqlServerAnomalyDetector.cs` + `SqlServerBaselineProvider.cs`) plus the shared `PerformanceMonitor.Analysis` (`FactScorer`, `FactAdvice`, and a new `AnomalyGate`). **(1) Baseline-quality gate:** the warmup gate now measures VARIANCE QUALITY, not just quantity â€” `BaselineBucket` carries `DistinctDays` (`COUNT(DISTINCT collection_time::DATE)`, summed exactly on the hour-only collapse and MAX-proxied on the flat collapse to avoid a second global query) and `IsTrustworthy` (tier-aware distinct-day minimums Full â‰¥3 / HourOnly â‰¥10 / Flat â‰¥3 â€” the flat collapse's MAX-of-hour-buckets distinct-day proxy is itself capped near ~5 in a 30-day window, so a â‰¥15 flat floor was structurally unreachable and left the flat trust branch dead â€” plus real dispersion), and bounded metrics (CPU/memory/IO) gain an absolute dispersion floor (`AbsStdDevFloor`, folded into `EffectiveStdDev`) so a variance-collapsed baseline can't manufacture a giant z. The shared `AnomalyGate.EvaluateZScore` centralizes the interaction-trap decision so the three detectors cannot drift: a trustworthy baseline trusts the z-score with the #1486 magnitude floor as a sanity ceiling; a thin/young baseline is NOT silenced but falls back to a HIGHER absolute-threshold bar (CPU â‰¥90%, memory â‰¥95%, batch â‰¥5000/s, sessions â‰¥500, query-duration â‰¥5s, IO â‰¥50ms â€” each above the matching #1486 floor). Because that fallback fire stores the real (small) z, `FactScorer` grades a low-quality fire off its absolute exceedance (peak Ã· the bar, carried on `AnomalyGate.ZDecision`) rather than the â€” now untrustworthy â€” z-score, floored so it clears the finding-surfacing threshold; without this the 2Ïƒ severity gate would zero it and a genuine young-store problem (e.g. memory 96%) would fire the gate but produce NO finding. **(2) Wait redesign:** the per-type `ANOMALY_WAIT_<type>` facts â€” which compared a per-hour per-type value to a per-interval all-types baseline (a ~240Ã— unit inflation) and missed a minority-but-real wait â€” become ONE `ANOMALY_WAIT_PROFILE`: the whole-server all-types wait ms/sec (interval derived via `LAG`, never an assumed cadence) vs the `WaitMsPerSec` baseline, with the top wait types named as `contrib_<TYPE>` metadata. Dashboard's `SqlServerMetricNames` gains `WaitMsPerSec` and its T-SQL baseline query. `FactScorer` gains a matching `ANOMALY_WAIT_PROFILE` arm and the wait slope + each detector's `DefaultRatioThreshold` are retuned to the honest per-second scale (4Ã— â†’ 0.5, 12Ã— â†’ 1.0); `FactAdvice` composes the profile from its named contributors. **(3) Honest no-baseline rendering:** the `100Ã—` sentinel on the blocking/deadlock ratio detectors is replaced with an `is_new` flag, and the composer now renders a first occurrence ("no baseline yet") instead of a fake "spiked to 100Ã—". The ratio/slope/fallback constants are labelled tunable and to be calibrated on the SQL2025/HammerDB box. This changes detection/alert behavior, so it ships with new tests across all three suites (thin-baseline fallback fires but a sub-bar z-spike is suppressed; a healthy baseline still trusts z; DistinctDays population + hour-only-sum/flat-max collapse; the wait profile emits one fact and captures a minority-but-real wait; the profile scoring ramp; a low-quality fallback fire is scored off its absolute exceedance rather than the zeroed z, so a young-store bounded-metric problem still surfaces). Stage B (incident dedup + the CXPACKET severity cap) is a separate later change. Lite + Dashboard + Darling
- **Lite and Darling: the default-trace collector can now suppress Object-DDL (schema-change) events, so a create/drop-happy workload no longer floods the System Events tab** ([#1485]) -- a new `collectSchemaChangeEvents` flag in `darling.json` (default true) gates the collector's `Object:Created` / `Altered` / `Deleted` slice, mirroring the full Dashboard's `@include_object_events`; e.g. HammerDB's TPC-H Query 15 creates and drops a `revenue` view thousands of times. Default-on keeps every SKU's behavior unchanged (Lite included), and it is a file-only knob (no schema migration).
- **Lite, Dashboard, and Darling: young-store anomaly noise -- absolute-magnitude floors and a sigma display cap** ([#1486]) -- on a young store the anomaly detector's z-scores run against a near-zero-variance baseline and explode, surfacing trivial values as "spikes" (e.g. "connection count spiked to 5", "query duration spiked to 1 ms", "36.3 min -- 5,389,105 sigma"). The detector -- triplicated across `Lite/Analysis/AnomalyDetector.cs`, `Dashboard/Analysis/SqlServerAnomalyDetector.cs`, and `Darling/PerformanceMonitor.Darling.Analysis/PgAnomalyDetector.cs` -- now applies tunable absolute-magnitude floors so a z-score against a thin baseline can't surface a trivial value: batch requests >= 500/sec, sessions >= 50, query duration >= 1s (1,000,000 us) total elapsed, memory pressure >= 90%, and the write-latency floor raised 5 -> 20 ms; each extends the metric's existing deviation-threshold guard (CPU keeps its prior `peakCpu < 50` floor). Every `deviation_sigma` metadata value is also capped at `Math.Min(dev, 25)` so a variance-collapsed baseline can't render millions-of-sigma. SAFE by construction: severity already saturates at 4 sigma, so a stored cap >= 4 changes only the displayed label, not the score, and the floors only suppress trivial spikes -- they never raise a real one. The memory floor is applied to the Dashboard too, since it collects memory (`install/14_collect_memory_stats.sql`) and runs a live `DetectMemoryAnomalies` -- the "Dashboard does not collect memory" comments in the Lite/Darling copies were stale and are corrected. Lite + Dashboard + Darling

The Memory Overview trend, both Memory Grants charts (sizing + activity), the Memory Clerks chart, and the four Query > Performance Trends charts (query / procedure / Query Store duration and execution count) were the remaining trend charts that never pinned the X-axis, so ScottPlot auto-fit with its default margin and left the same empty space at both edges. Each now pins to the selected window with `SetLimitsX` right after `DateTimeTicksBottomDateChange()`, exactly like the CPU/File I/O charts -- in both the populated and empty-data paths for the dense per-interval Memory charts, and in the populated path for the four Query-Trend charts (whose empty state keeps its existing "No Data" placeholder). `ViewerServerTab.Memory.cs` / `ViewerServerTab.QueryTrends.cs` (Darling) and `ServerTab.Charts.cs` / `ServerTab.Pickers.cs` (Lite -- the Memory Clerks chart lives in the picker file). Separately, the four Blocking-Stats charts (Darling) do pin the window but plot only the per-minute buckets that had a blocking/deadlock event, so when activity stops the connected line ends early while the axis runs on to the window's right edge; each series is now padded with a zero point at `rangeStart`/`rangeEnd` -- the same zero-baseline idiom the sibling Blocking/Deadlock Trend charts already use -- so the line spans the whole window (no activity = 0 ms). The reader stays ascending on purpose: the metric-trend chart plots the same `_historyData` list in reader order and the "from X to Y" summary reads `First()`/`Last()`, so flipping the SQL would render the chart backwards and invert the summary. The fix adds a grid-view-only descending `SortDescription` on the `CollectionTime` `DateTime` (guarded so a user's later header-click sort survives) plus `SortMemberPath="CollectionTime"` / `SortDirection="Descending"` on the Collection Time column (whose cell binds the formatted string), so the grid shows most-recent-first while the chart and summary keep their chronological order -- matching the convention that a grid's default sort is always descending, and bringing the three drill grids into parity with their parent grids. The same audit also flips the FinOps **Database Sizes** grid (`FinOpsDatabaseSizesDataGrid`) from alphabetical (`database_name, file_type_desc, file_name`) to `total_size_mb DESC` (biggest files first) -- a capacity view surfaces the largest files, accepting that files interleave across databases. That reader's `ORDER BY` is changed directly (rather than a grid-view-only sort) because the grid is its only order-sensitive consumer: the utilization free-space math and the dormant-database recommendation's cost share only `Sum` the rows, and the neighbouring "Allocated vs Used" chart is a separate read (`GetDatabaseSizeSummaryAsync`, already size-descending). It is a plain `config`-schema registry table (not a collector, so no `CollectorScheduleDefaults` horizon; not a hypertable, so no `drop_chunks`), so the daily sweep now purges it via the same batched `DELETE` idiom as `collection_log`, on its `alert_time` column, at a new `AlertHistoryRetentionDays = 90` horizon (a quarter -- generous for a low-volume audit trail, but bounded). Failure-isolated like every sibling table (a failed statement is logged and counted, the sweep continues; `PurgeAsync` never throws at the daily caller). Covered by a pure unit test (the 90-day constant plus the batched `alert_time` DELETE shape) and the gated live-Postgres end-to-end purge (a 100-day row goes, a 1-hour row survives)

- **Darling: schema V22 adds a supporting index for the FinOps Index Analysis read** ([#1477]) -- the viewer's Index Analysis reader picks the newest snapshot per index with `SELECT DISTINCT ON (database_id, object_id, index_id) ... WHERE server_id = $1 ORDER BY database_id, object_id, index_id, collection_time DESC` (no time bound, so it walks the whole per-server history), but the only `index_object_stats` index (`idx_index_object_stats_object`, from V1) leads `(server_id, database_name, ...)` -- a database_NAME vs the query's database_ID mismatch that cannot satisfy the `DISTINCT ON` ordering, forcing a full sort of the server's rows. V22 adds `idx_index_object_stats_latest (server_id, database_id, object_id, index_id, collection_time DESC)`, matching the read's exact key so it reads in index order without a sort; it is additive (the V1 index still serves the anomaly-detector self-joins that key `database_name`). `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS` so a V21 store upgrades idempotently and a fresh store gets it too; `index_object_stats` is a TimescaleDB hypertable, so Timescale applies the index across its chunks. `StorageVersion.SchemaVersion` is bumped 21 to 22, and the viewer's connect-time schema-skew probe gains a matching V22 sentinel (via `pg_indexes`, since indexes are not listed in `information_schema`) so a correctly-migrated V22 store is not falsely gated

- **Lite and Darling: "Current Waits" now honors the ignored-waits filter, matching Wait Stats** ([#1476]) -- the waiting-task duration chart (and Lite's `get_waiting_tasks` MCP tool) showed benign wait types the user had deliberately ignored, while the Wait Stats view filtered them out. The shared `WaitingTasksCollector` was ported from the SQL collector (`install/37_collect_waiting_tasks.sql`, which filters via `config.ignored_wait_types`) but dropped the ignored-wait skip, keeping only the database-exclusion splice. `WaitingTasksCollector.ReadAsync` now skips `context.IgnoredWaitTypes` exactly like `WaitStatsCollector.ReadAsync`, fixing collection in BOTH active SKUs (Lite feeds `ignored_wait_types.json`, Darling feeds `IgnoredWaitDefaults.All`); Lite's `GetWaitingTaskTrendAsync` and `GetWaitingTasksAsync` additionally exclude the ignored types at DISPLAY time via `IgnoredWaitTypes.BuildExclusionClause` (the #1240 belt-and-suspenders) so waiting tasks already in the DuckDB â€” collected before a type was ignored, since Lite's list is user-editable at runtime â€” don't resurface. The Darling viewer reads are intentionally left filter-free, matching Darling's Wait Stats, which deliberately applies no per-user display filter. Pinned by a new `WaitingTasksCollectorDefinitionTests.ReadAsync_FiltersIgnoredWaitTypes` (a benign `WAITFOR` on a user session is dropped, lock/scheduler waits kept)
- **Lite and Dashboard: the analysis-findings retention purge is now actually scheduled** ([#1471]) â€” both apps' finding stores declared a 30-day `CleanupOldFindingsAsync` (behind `AnalysisService.CleanupAsync`) that nothing ever called, so `analysis_findings` never got its intended rolling retention. Dashboard's per-server `config.analysis_findings` grew unbounded; Lite's DuckDB table was bounded only incidentally when a 512 MB size trip reset the whole database â€” losing ALL findings, not just aged ones (it is not in `ArchiveService.ArchivableTables`, so routine archival never touched it). Lite now runs the purge from a daily `CollectionBackgroundService` maintenance tick (mirroring the parquet-retention tick); Dashboard runs it once per 24h per server inside `AnalysisScheduler` (each monitored server owns its own findings table). Mirrors the Darling service, which already documents this exact gap and schedules the same 30-day cleanup in its daily purge. Covered by a Lite real-DuckDB test that the now-live `AnalysisService.CleanupAsync` purges, plus a Dashboard offline pin of the retention SQL (extracted to a `CleanupOldFindingsSql` const, mirroring the Darling twin)
- **Darling: schema V14 refreshes every `v_*` passthrough view so a store upgraded across a column-adding migration serves the new columns** ([#1262]) â€” PostgreSQL freezes a view's `SELECT *` column list at `CREATE` time, so the passthrough views created in V4-V6 (and V10-V13) did not include columns a later migration `ADD`ed to their base tables: the V7 deferred-plan-capture columns on `blocked_process_reports`/`deadlocks` and the V9 server-inventory/cost columns. A fresh store was always correct (its views were created from the current table shapes); only a store upgraded across those boundaries served stale views. PR #1376 discovered this and worked around it for the plan columns by reading the base tables directly â€” this migration closes the root cause by re-issuing `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_x AS SELECT * FROM x` for all 30 passthrough views (the list generated from `PgSchemaGenerator`'s authoritative `AllPassthroughViews`, so it cannot drift from the collector catalog), which re-expands each `SELECT *` to the base table's current shape. Safe because every post-V4 change was an append-only `ADD COLUMN` â€” the one alteration `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` permits â€” and V14 runs after the V8 schema split, so the bare names resolve through `search_path = collect, config, public` and replace each view in place. Applied idempotently on the service's next start; a fresh store re-installs identical definitions. **Lite's DuckDB is unaffected:** although DuckDB pins `SELECT *` at view creation identically (in fact more strictly â€” it errors on a shape-changed view rather than silently truncating), Lite re-creates every view via `CREATE OR REPLACE` in `CreateArchiveViewsAsync` on every startup, so its views self-heal each launch and were never stale. Pinned by ungated SQL-shape tests: the plan-bearing views (`v_blocked_process_reports`, `v_deadlocks`) refresh, plus a divergence guard asserting the refresh set equals every view any migration creates
- **Darling viewer: the CPU series now aligns with every other timeline on non-UTC servers** ([#1262]) â€” `cpu_utilization_stats.sample_time` is the monitored server's LOCAL wall clock (`SYSDATETIME()` on the server, minus each ring-buffer sample's age), but the viewer's CPU read handed it to `ToLocalTime`, which assumes naive-UTC input â€” so both consumers, the CPU inner tab and the Overview's correlated CPU lane, plotted the whole CPU series shifted by the server's UTC offset relative to every `collection_time`-based lane (e.g. seven to eight hours off on a Pacific-time server, offset -7/-8). `GetCpuUtilizationAsync` now de-skews `sample_time` to naive UTC inside the read: within a collection batch (keyed on the shared `collection_time` â€” `collection_id` is a per-row column in the Darling store, not a batch id) the newest sample is at most ~1 minute older than the collection instant, so `round(MAX(sample_time) over the batch - collection_time)` to the nearest 15 minutes recovers the server's UTC offset (covering half/quarter-hour zones and absorbing the sub-minute anchor age), and subtracting it turns each local `sample_time` into true naive UTC. A UTC server yields a zero offset, byte-identical to the prior read. Pinned by an ungated SQL-shape test (window MAX + 15-minute rounding) and a gated live-Postgres round-trip that plants Pacific (UTC-7 and UTC-8), India (UTC+5:30, a half-hour zone), and UTC batches and asserts each lands back on its `collection_time`

- **Darling: schema V5 adds the five missing passthrough views** ([#1262]) -- `v_running_jobs`, `v_server_config`, `v_database_scoped_config`, `v_trace_flags`, and `v_collection_log` complete the `v_*` twin of Lite's DuckDB view layer, so the viewer copy-parity ports of Running Jobs, Configuration, Daily Summary, and Collection Health read SQL byte-identical to Lite's (tables existed since V1/V2; views only, applied idempotently on the service's next start)

- **Darling: managed PostgreSQL now sizes background workers for TimescaleDB's compression jobs** ([#1262]) â€” PostgreSQL's default `max_worker_processes = 8` could not launch the 26 per-hypertable compression policy jobs, producing "failed to start a background worker" warning storms in the server log and failing most policy runs (caught live on a fresh managed instance: 21 failed vs 7 successful runs in `timescaledb_information.job_stats`). The managed bootstrap appends a second versioned conf block per the TimescaleDB sizing guidance (`timescaledb.max_background_workers = 28`, `max_worker_processes = 40`); clusters initialized before the sizing existed self-heal the conf on their next start, effective at the next PostgreSQL restart

- **Lite, Dashboard, and Darling: muting a finding "across all servers" now actually mutes everywhere** ([#1262]) â€” the MCP `mute_analysis_finding` tool's all-servers path wrote `server_id = 0`, but every muted-registry reader filters `server_id = <server> OR server_id IS NULL`, so a 0-scoped row matched no real server (server ids are name hashes, never 0) and the all-servers mute was a silent no-op. The tool now persists `server_id = NULL` â€” the canonical global marker readers already honor â€” and every reader additionally treats a legacy `server_id = 0` row as global, so mutes written before this fix keep working. Lite (DuckDB `FindingStore`) and Darling (`PgFindingStore`) collapse the 0 sentinel to NULL on write; the Dashboard MCP tool has no all-servers path (it always resolves a concrete server), so only its reader gains the legacy-0 compatibility. Covered in all three suites â€” Lite's real-DuckDB `FindingStore` tests (all-servers write persists NULL, legacy-0 honored, per-server mutes don't leak), the Dashboard reader-SQL pin, and Darling's ungated SQL pins plus gated live-Postgres round-trips (the all-servers tool persisting NULL, and the NULL / legacy-0 / current-server / other-server read spans)

## [3.1.0] - 2026-06-28

### Added

- **Lite and Dashboard: a shared block-chain viewer reconstructs the full apex â†’ victim blocking tree** ([#1207]) â€” right-click *View Block Chain* (or double-click a row) on the Dashboard **Locking** / Lite **Blocking** grids opens a focused graph of the clicked session's blocking chain, rooted at its apex (lead blocker) with the full hierarchy of waiters beneath it. Node cards lead with session identity (login/host/app), the contended object, and the SQL text rather than a bare SPID; the clicked node auto-selects and scrolls into view; and the canvas has zoom/pan/fit plus a properties panel. Reconstruction, tree-building (DAG â†’ tree, cycle-safe), and layout are pure and unit-tested in shared `PerformanceMonitor.Common` (`BlockingChainModel` / `BlockingChainTreeBuilder` / `BlockingChainLayout`) with the WPF shell in `PerformanceMonitor.Ui/BlockingChainControl`, so the two apps can't drift, and the fetch/reconstruct/build runs off the UI thread. The chain is picked edge-precisely around the clicked row's own `event_time` (Â±5 min) so double-clicking any visible row reliably opens that event's chain, and sessions are keyed by `(monitor_loop, spid, ecid)` â€” mirroring `sp_HumanEventsBlockViewer` â€” with `(spid, ecid)` and SPID-only fallbacks so historical rows still resolve. Covered by `BlockingChainTreeBuilderTests` and `BlockingChainLayoutTests`, with `BlockingChainReconstructorTests` mirrored in both suites
- **Lite and Dashboard: a shared deadlock graph viewer shows the waits-for cycles** ([#1216]) â€” right-click *View Deadlock Graph* (or double-click a row) on the deadlock grid renders the deadlock as a **cycle view** of the waits-for graph â€” not an SSMS process|resource bipartite graph â€” because a real deadlock is typically a bundle of independent small cycles rather than one large N-cycle. Each process card leads with SPID + statement + lock + wait; the rolled-back victim gets a red border and a VICTIM badge; directional arrows are labeled by the contended resource (resolved to an object name from the deadlock XML, e.g. `PAGE hammerdb_tpcc.dbo.new_order`); and each independent cycle is framed in its own dashed *Cycle N* box with the count noted in the summary. The parser/model/layout live in shared `PerformanceMonitor.Common` (`DeadlockGraphParser` / `DeadlockGraphModel` / `DeadlockGraphLayout` â€” marks all victims, handles the Azure event wrapper, parallelism self-edges, and a nameless-resource fallback, and never throws) with the control in `PerformanceMonitor.Ui/DeadlockGraphControl`, and parsing runs off the UI thread. Covered by `DeadlockGraphParserTests` and `DeadlockGraphLayoutTests` against real 2/5/8-process golden samples
- **Lite and Dashboard: an always-on DMV blocking-snapshot fallback keeps blocking visible without the blocked-process report** ([#1227]) â€” a new `dmv_blocking_snapshots` collector captures point-in-time blocking from `sys.dm_os_waiting_tasks` + `sys.dm_exec_*`, independent of the `blocked_process_report` Extended Event (which only fires when `blocked process threshold` is set â€” off by default, and unsettable via `sp_configure` on AWS RDS). It feeds the same source-agnostic chain reconstructor, so the blocking grid, the chain viewer, the flat top-blocking drill-down, the slicer/trend, and the count/badge surfaces all stay populated even when no blocked-process reports were captured. DMV rows merge **BPR-preferred** through the shared `PerformanceMonitor.Analysis/BlockingPairRowMerge` (synthetic negative `monitor_loop` so DMV episodes never collide with real ones); counts use `COALESCE(NULLIF(bpr,0), dmv)` and bucketed surfaces add DMV rows only where no BPR exists in the window, so a server with both sources never double-counts, and a *Source* badge marks each row's origin. The collector applies layered minimum-wait floors by contention class (LCK 2s, PAGELATCH 0.5s, PAGEIOLATCH 1s, RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE 5s) to cut noise, and the slicer/drill-down probe for the table so a not-yet-upgraded server degrades to BPR-only instead of erroring. Covered by `BlockingPairRowMergeTests` in both suites
- **Lite and Dashboard: analysis findings are grouped into trackable incidents on the Recommendations surface** ([#1214]) â€” instead of a flat, severity-sorted sea of cards, the recommendation surfaces group findings by a stable `incident_id` into one collapsible report per incident (header = the primary/highest-severity finding + finding count + severity), with each card keeping its own advice / Copy / Apply. The id is a fingerprint of the incident's primary finding's root key + database, scoped to the server, so the **same recurring incident keeps the same id across runs** (trackable, not a per-run GUID); findings are clustered into incidents by connected components over the analysis relationship graph's active edges, so a run's genuinely-distinct problems get distinct incidents while related facets (a plan regression that's really part of a CPU incident, or a THREADPOOLâ†’LCK blocking-driven thread exhaustion) merge into one. The `incident_id` is persisted in both stores (Lite analysis-schema, Dashboard `config.analysis_findings`) and emitted per-finding by the MCP `analyze_server` / `get_analysis_findings`, alongside a "what else fired in this window" cross-reference. Covered by `IncidentIdTests`, `InferenceEngineTests`, and the recommendations view-model tests in both suites
- **Lite and Dashboard: FinOps storage analysis becomes an object-growth â†’ index drill with in-grid heatmaps** ([#1138]) â€” the standalone *Object Sizes & Growth* and *Index Usage* tabs are replaced by a **Storage Growth â†’ object â†’ index** drill: double-click a database to its object-growth heatmap (rows = top-N objects by reserved-MB growth over the window, X = daily buckets, color = reserved MB on a per-column log scale) with a companion grid, then double-click an object for its per-index size + usage. The *Locking & Contention* tab becomes a heatmap-in-grid â€” the four wait-time columns are shaded per-column by their wait category's hue (Lock / Buffer Latch / Buffer IO) with the numbers still visible â€” plus a database selector and a per-index lock/latch drill. The top-N ranking, long â†’ matrix pivot, and color-scale math are pure and shared (`PerformanceMonitor.Common/FinOpsHeatmap`, `PerformanceMonitor.Ui/FinOpsHeatmapRenderer`, `HeatIntensityToBrushConverter`) so both apps render identically, and the read layer ranks the top-N cheaply before series-scanning only those rows (DB-scoped on the covering index's lead column to avoid the [#1135] uncovered scan). The existing `GetObjectSizeGrowthAsync` / `GetIndexUsageAsync` stay for the MCP. Covered by `FinOpsHeatmapBuilderTests` (plus Lite integration tests) in both suites
- **Lite and Dashboard: per-server override for the alert delivery mode** ([#1236]) â€” the per-event vs. summary delivery mode ([#1141]) can now be overridden per server (e.g. Per-event for one noisy prod box while the global default stays Summary). `ServerConnection` gains a nullable `AlertDeliveryModeOverride` persisted in the existing `servers.json` (no new store; null inherits the global), the Add/Edit Server dialog in both apps gets an *Alert delivery* combo (Use global setting / Summary / Per-event), and a shared `AlertDeliveryModeResolver` centralizes the precedence so the two apps can't drift. Covered by `AlertDeliveryModeOverrideTests` in both suites
- **Lite and Dashboard: MCP tools return a structured status envelope for non-data outcomes** ([#1224]) â€” `McpHelpers.Status(status, message, hints?)` lets an LLM client distinguish a true negative (`empty`) from a bad input (`not_collected`) from a transient substrate gap (`unavailable`) instead of parsing prose, routed through every data-miss return across both apps' MCP tools (102 sites / 38 files). Lite's `get_perfmon_trend` / `get_wait_trend` return the actually-collected counters / wait types as hints, and `analyze_server`'s no-findings result becomes `empty`. Setup, validation, and resolution messages and the data-returning success paths are unchanged. Covered by `McpStatusEnvelopeTests`
- **Lite and Dashboard: in-app plan navigation on every query-identifying surface** ([#1184]) â€” *View Plan* (open the collected/cached plan) and *Get Actual Plan* (re-execute for a fresh actual plan) are now available from every view that identifies a single query in both apps â€” the history/drill-down windows (Query Stats, Query Store, Procedure, Wait drill-down), the comparison grids (whose menu items previously no-opped because the switch lacked the comparison-item cases), and the FinOps High-Impact / Expensive-Queries grids â€” via a shared `PlanNavigationController` so the confirm/cancel/busy/error handling lives once and the two apps stay in parity
- **Full Dashboard: a "Collection Stopped" alert for when the collector itself goes dark** ([#1246]) â€” the app tracked collection *health* (did data arrive?) but never collection *state*, so disabling the SQL Agent collector jobs was silent: the Dashboard kept looking healthy â€” calmer, even, since the live cards read zero rows from the `collect.*` tables â€” until a collector aged into STALE on the Collection Health tab after 24 hours. A new app-side check that survives the collector being off (it is the collector that fills every other table) now watches two things: a live read of `msdb.dbo.sysjobs.enabled` for the `PerformanceMonitor%` jobs (the immediate, specific cause) and a `config.collection_log` freshness backstop (no run in 30+ minutes, which also catches the Agent service being stopped or collectors silently erroring). It surfaces as a proactive "Collection Stopped" tray/email alert â€” a new `NotifyOnCollectionStopped` setting (default on), with a "Collection Resumed" clear and the usual cooldown/mute, mirroring the Capture Down pattern â€” plus a banner on the Collection Health tab, so it shows immediately instead of only after the 24-hour STALE lag. The msdb read is gated off on Azure SQL Database and degrades gracefully where msdb is restricted (e.g. AWS RDS / no `SQLAgentReaderRole`), so it never reports "disabled" when it simply could not look. The decision logic is extracted to `DatabaseService.DecideCollectionStopped` and unit-tested (9 cases). Full edition only â€” Lite runs its own in-app scheduler, not Agent jobs.

### Changed

- **Lite and Dashboard: the recommendation engine's operator advice is rebuilt to be sourced and composed from your server's own facts** ([#1189], [#1196], [#1197], [#1198], [#1203], [#1244]) â€” the advice on every Recommendation (headline, investigation, remediation) was largely unsourced folklore that hedged ("maybe, ifâ€¦") and pointed at MCP tool names (`get_*`) instead of stating the measured number. It now **composes from the collected fact set at analysis time**: each of the 56 advice blocks states your server's actual values â€” current MAXDOP/CTFP, max server memory, the RCSI-off database count, the dominant lock mode, the SOS signal-wait share, the lead blocker's identity, and the named contended object (`dbo.Orders` / `index IX_â€¦`, via a new `Fact.ObjectName` carrier the collectors had been dropping) â€” and each remediation states the co-fired findings that actually fired rather than a bag of generic guesses. Tool names, internal field names, and the speculative "bag of tricks" are stripped from both the composed path and the static fallbacks, and the composed advice is frozen into each finding's story at analysis time so it reads identically in the apps and the MCP. Covered by `FactAdviceComposeTests` and `FactAdviceCorrectnessTests` in both suites. (A larger prose rewrite is planned for a future release.)
- **Lite and Dashboard: click a chart's legend key (or a series line) to isolate that series** â€” on any multi-series trend chart, left-clicking a series' built-in legend key â€” or its line in the plot â€” now dims every other series and auto-fits the Y axis to the clicked one, so a wait type (or metric) that sits flat against the axis underneath the big lines becomes readable. Clicking it again, clicking a different series, or double-clicking (autoscale) restores the full view. It is a transient view toggle only: it never changes the picker selection and never refetches or deletes data, and any re-render (picker/time-range change or a background poll) resets it. The whole mechanic lives in the shared `PerformanceMonitor.Ui/ChartHoverHelper` that every dynamic-legend chart in both apps already routes its series through â€” so the two apps can't drift â€” and the Y-fit transiently clears then restores Dashboard's `LockedVertical` axis rule so the fit actually sticks. The dim uses each series' own identity color (so it works in Dark/Light/CoolBreeze), and clicking a memory-pressure **bar** legend key is intentionally a no-op (stacked bars are deferred). Covered by `ChartClickIsolateTests` in both suites
- **Lite and Dashboard: alert payloads carry a stable dedup fingerprint and involved-object list** ([#1140]) â€” deadlock and blocking alerts (plus query/job/disk) now attach a deterministic, server-scoped fingerprint and the list of involved objects, computed in the shared `PerformanceMonitor.Notifications/AlertFingerprint.cs` (sorted, literal-stripped, excluding volatile fields) and grouped into `AlertContext.Incidents` via `IncidentGrouping`. This gives every downstream consumer â€” cooldown ([#1154]), per-event delivery ([#1141]), and restart dedup ([#1145]) â€” a stable key for "the same incident" instead of re-alerting on cosmetically-different text. Wired into both apps' alert engines; covered by `AlertFingerprintTests`, `IncidentGroupingTests`, and `AlertIncidentRenderTests`
- **Lite and Dashboard: optional per-event notification mode for deadlocks and blocking** ([#1141]) â€” alerts can now be delivered as one message per distinct incident instead of the default batched per-cycle summary, controlled by a new `AlertDeliveryMode` (Summary | PerEvent) setting plus `AlertPerEventMaxPerCycle` (default 10, with a "+N more" overflow) in both apps' Settings. Per-event cards keep the full forensic detail and a numeric current value. Built on the [#1140] incident grouping; covered by `PerEventNotificationTests`. (A per-server override is tracked as a fast-follow â€” Dashboard has no per-server settings store yet.)
- **Lite and Dashboard: the low-disk (Volume Free Space) alert is now severity-graded instead of always INFO** ([#1136]) â€” the metric name was absent from the shared severity map, so every low-disk alert fell through to the default INFO tier (blue, lowest severity) regardless of how full the volume was. A volume nearing full stops data/log file growth â€” transactions fail and the database can go into recovery/suspect â€” so this under-prioritized a potentially critical condition, including for downstream severity-based webhook routing (Teams/Slack). The alert now renders **WARNING** for a normal breach and **CRITICAL** when the worst breached volume is critically low (â‰¤ 3% free **or** â‰¤ 2 GB free â€” a second, lower tier beneath the user-configured fire threshold). The critical grading lives in the shared `LowDiskAlertGate.IsCriticallyLow`, and the tier rides through to the email badge/accent, Teams card, and Slack sidebar via an `AlertContext.SeverityOverride`, so the metric name (hence mute rules, cooldown, and Alert-History matching) is unchanged. The existing "notify only on a fresh or worsening breach" firing rule is untouched â€” this is purely the severity classification. Fixed identically in both apps. Covered by `AlertSeverityTests` and `LowDiskAlertGateTests`
- **Lite and Dashboard: the execution-plan viewer is now one shared control** ([#1205]) â€” Dashboard and Lite each carried a near-identical 6-file `PlanViewerControl`; the plan parsing/layout/analysis already lived in the shared `PerformanceMonitor.PlanAnalysis`, so only the WPF shell was duplicated. That shell is now a single `PerformanceMonitor.Ui.PlanViewerControl` referenced by both apps, so it can no longer drift. Two host-visible effects: (1) **Lite's multi-statement picker becomes a sortable grid** â€” for a plan with more than one statement, Lite previously used a `Statements:` dropdown and now shows Dashboard's collapsible **Statements** panel (a sortable grid of #, query text, CPU/Elapsed/UDF or estimated cost, and Critical/Warning counts, with right-click â†’ Copy Query Text), so you can sort a batch by cost or runtime to find the heavy statement; single-statement plans are unchanged (no panel). (2) The shared control parses and analyzes **off the UI thread**, so opening a large showplan no longer briefly freezes the window. The theme-change handler also moves to a `Cleanup()`-at-teardown lifecycle in both apps â€” it is no longer detached on `Unloaded` (which a `TabControl` raises on every tab switch, the previous Dashboard behavior that could leave a backgrounded plan tab no longer re-theming); each app now calls `Cleanup()` at every real teardown (plan window/tab close, server-tab close, and the malformed-XML error path)
- **Lite and Dashboard: "Show Active Queries at This Time" right-click drill-down now works on every resource chart** ([#1208]) â€” the chart drill-down (right-click a point to jump to Active Queries scoped to that Â±30-minute window, originally [#682]) was wired on only a subset of charts and had drifted between the two apps. A full audit of every chart surfaced three problems, all fixed: (1) the Dashboard **Resources/TempDB tab** drill-down was dead plumbing â€” the control defined the `AddDrillDown` mechanism and a `ChartDrillDownRequested` event that the server tab even subscribed to, but never wired a single chart, so none of its 11 charts could drill down; (2) the TempDB **Allocated MB** chart (both apps) and Lite's **Memory Pressure Events** chart had no right-click menu at all (no save/export *or* drill-down) because they were never registered â€” they now get the full menu plus a new hover helper so the click can resolve a timestamp; (3) bidirectional parity drift â€” Lite lacked it on Memory Clerks/Grants/Pressure and Current/Lock Waits while Dashboard had them, and Dashboard lacked it on TempDB Stats while Lite had it. The drill-down is now present on every time-series resource chart in both apps (memory clerks/grants/pressure, tempdb size/stats/file-I/O latency, file-I/O latency + throughput, perfmon, current waits, and â€” Dashboard only â€” session/latch/spinlock stats and plan cache; Lite's Lock Wait routes to *Show Blocking* to match Dashboard). The query/procedure/Query Store/execution **duration-trend** charts are intentionally excluded because the gridâ†’slicer overlay already routes there, as are Collector Duration and the system-health event charts. Lite consolidates the new navigation into one shared `OnActiveQueriesDrillDown` handler rather than duplicating the existing CPU/Memory/TempDB drill-down bodies
- **Lite and Dashboard: the Overview correlated-timeline lanes get the same Active Queries drill-down** ([#1210]) â€” follow-on to [#1208]. The five synchronized lanes (CPU, Wait Stats, Blocking, Memory, File I/O) are a deliberately stripped-chrome view that disables all chart mouse input for its shared crosshair, so they had no right-click at all â€” and in Lite that control *is* the **Overview / default landing tab** (Dashboard's 2Ã—2 Overview grid already drilled, so this also closes a cross-app gap). Each lane now has a minimal right-click menu with just *Show Active Queries at This Time*; because pan/zoom is disabled the clicked time is read straight from the X axis, and it routes to the same Â±30-minute Active Queries navigation as every other chart. The synchronized crosshair is unaffected â€” it is mouse-move driven, independent of the right-click handler
- **Dashboard: the Queries and Resource tabs load much faster** ([#1181], [#1182], [#1190]) â€” opening the Queries tab took 3â€“9s under load. The heavy sub-tabs (heatmap, regressions, patterns) now lazy-load like the big grids; first-load, tab-switch, and time-range changes refresh only the *visible* tab instead of all six at once (which saturated the connection pool); the Query/Procedure/Query Store grids drop from `TOP (500)` to `TOP (50)` (matching Lite, ~10x less query-text decompression); and the large plan / deadlock-graph / blocked-process XML is deferred out of the grid queries and fetched on demand â€” so Query Stats now opens in well under a second
- **Lite and Dashboard: the Active Queries view refreshes when you open it** ([#1183]) â€” the sub-tab previously showed the last-loaded snapshot until the next timer tick; it now re-runs the live snapshot fetch when it becomes active (Dashboard had no auto-refresh on it at all), guarded so the wait/chart/heatmap drill-downs that select Active Queries with *filtered* data aren't clobbered by the refresh
- **Lite and Dashboard: resolved/cleared tray toasts are themed to match the condition cards** ([#1186]) â€” *Blocking Cleared*, *CPU Resolved*, etc. went through a plain unthemed Windows balloon while the triggering alert used the themed card, so a resolution looked nothing like the alert it resolved.
